name: Eternal Victory
description: Valerian was captured by Shapur. The victory was such a great one that Shapur decided to carve a scene of Valerian's defeat on a mountain. So he had to find the best place to make his victory eternal! He decided to visit all n cities of Persia to find the best available mountain, but after the recent war he was too tired and didn't want to traverse a lot. So he wanted to visit each of these n cities at least once with smallest possible traverse. Persian cities are connected with bidirectional roads. You can go from any city to any other one using these roads and there is a unique path between each two cities. All cities are numbered 1 to n . Shapur is currently in the city 1 and he wants to visit all other cities with minimum possible traverse. He can finish his travels in any city. Help Shapur find how much He should travel.
input_specification: First line contains a single natural number n ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 10 5 ) — the amount of cities. Next n - 1 lines contain 3 integer numbers each x i , y i and w i ( 1 ≤ x i , y i ≤ n , 0 ≤ w i ≤ 2 × 10 4 ). x i and y i are two ends of a road and w i is the length of that road.
output_specification: A single integer number, the minimal length of Shapur's travel. Please, do not use %lld specificator to read or write 64-bit integers in C++. It is preffered to use cout (also you may use %I64d ).
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 61D — Eternal Victory [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
